Lessons.Title: Ways to Look at Figures
ExplanationParagraphs:
Learning goal: You will analyze two-dimensional figures and sort them into different categories based on your attributes.
In grades 2 and 3, you studied some attributes of two-dimensional figures. In a previous unit, you investigated lines, rays, and segments, and drew and measured angles. You learned what it means when two lines or segments are parallel and perpendicular.

2021 source lesson activities: Warm-up: Which One Doesn’t Belong: Geometric Figures (10 minutes); Activity 1: Card Sort: Shapes (20 minutes); Activity 2: Guess the Category (15 minutes); Cool-down: What Do They Have in Common? (5 minutes)
Source-goal geometric reasoning: Sort figures by verifiable attributes: number of sides, right angles, equal lengths, parallel sides and symmetry.

Edulytics worked explanation: Inspect all original shape cards before grouping. List at least one shared attribute for each category and test every member. Explain why a figure might fit more than one mathematically valid category.
First-party Edulytics Cool-down (not gated original): Sort a square and a non-square rectangle by right angles and equal side lengths.
Original student diagrams, teacher card sorting, paper folding, and physical drawings require figure-by-figure / teacher validation.

Unit 8 original source introduces shape classification using attributes. The four Which One Doesn't Belong figures have different properties: one right-angle triangle and quadrilaterals including a parallelogram and trapezoid. Source Activity 1 Card Sort: Shapes asks 3–5 categories with written sticky-note titles. Activity 2 Guess the Category asks partner to supply 3 examples and 3 nonexamples. Categories may overlap and require justified source card sorting; do not infer a single answer key from excerpted diagram descriptions.

WorkedExamples.Title: First-party shape category reasoning
WorkedExamples.Question: Can a square fit both the quadrilateral and rectangle categories?
WorkedExamples.Method: Check definitions rather than the drawing orientation.
Steps: Square has four sides, so is a quadrilateral.
Square has four right angles, so is a rectangle.
A figure can belong to several valid attribute categories.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Assuming a drawing, classification or calculation is correct from appearance alone.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treating card sorting as a unique rigid classification.
